title: Roberts Travel Group joins Leicester City
article_text:
Leicestershire-based Roberts Travel Group has joined Leicester City as club partner and coach supplier until the end of the 2026/27 season.

The local operator will run the club’s away supporter coach travel, alongside a range of other transport and travel operations, including coaches for the boys’ and girls’ academies. Supporters will also see the brand across matchday and Fan Zone entertainment and on the club’s digital platforms.

The deal follows last week’s agreement with recruitment platform Bossjob, which became the club’s front-of-shirt partner for the rest of the season.

Russell Jones, Commercial Director at Leicester City, said, “We’re delighted to welcome Roberts Travel Group as an Official Partner and our Official Coach Supplier. It’s fantastic to have another successful local business join our Club as an Official Partner. Roberts provide such a valuable service to local people – from transporting thousands of children to school to providing unique holiday trips across the country.“

“For Leicester City, Roberts continue to provide coaches for our boys and girls academies, and our away coaches, helping fans get around the country to support the team. Thank you to the team at Roberts Travel Group for taking this next step by becoming an Official Partner. We’re really excited to see how we can continue to grow our partnership in the months and years ahead.”

Alex Niemczyk, Managing Director at Roberts Travel Group, said, “We’re incredibly proud to become an Official Partner and Official Coach Supplier of Leicester City. As a Leicestershire-based business, this partnership is particularly special to us, and we are delighted to be working alongside a club with such a strong connection to its local community.“

“At Roberts Travel Group, we understand just how important football is to fans, and we are committed to providing safe, reliable and comfortable travel experiences for supporters following their team. We look forward to building a successful partnership with Leicester City and playing our part in helping fans enjoy their matchday experience.”

title: TV4 nets early extension for SHL rights
article_text:
TV4, the Swedish Telia-owned commercial broadcaster, has secured an early extension to its domestic rights agreement covering ice hockey’s top-tier Swedish Hockey League until the 2035-36 season.

The six-year agreement represents an early extension between the pair, with their current contract running through 2029-30.

Combine business intelligence and editorial excellence to reach engaged professionals across 36 leading media platforms.

Citing sources close to the deal, Swedish news outlet Aftonbladet said the new contract represents a minor increase on the current agreement, which gives the 14 SHL clubs SEK50 million ($4.86 million) each in revenue per season.

SHL chief executive Jenny Silfverstrand said: “We are incredibly happy to be able to continue our good and long-term cooperation with TV4.

“TV4 has been an important partner for SHL for many years, and we share the ambition to develop SHL into the world's best ice hockey experience. Regardless of whether you are in the arena or watching the game from the TV couch.”

The deal builds on TV4 long-standing broadcast partnership with SHL, having first aired SHL, then known as Elitserien, in 1994 before securing rights in 2008. Since then, the broadcaster has served as the league’s exclusive broadcast home.

Parent company Telia signed a six-year extension to its rights deal to provide coverage of the league between the 2018-19 to 2023-24 seasons. During this cycle, Telia housed its SHL broadcasts under TV4’s pay-TV and streaming subsidiary C More.

In 2020, Telia struck another early six-year extension, taking its contract through 2029-30.

TV4 chief executive Mathias Berg added: “TV4 has a fantastic development with strong digital growth and record levels on TV4 Play. Behind the successes lies a clear strategy and long-term investments in content that engages all of Sweden.

“SHL is an important part of our sports position and the long-term agreement is further proof that our strategy is yielding results and strengthens us in our ambition to become Sweden's largest streaming service.”

Alongside SHL, TV4 holds rights in Sweden to domestic ice hockey’s second-tier HockeyAllsvenskan in a deal running between 2026-27 and 2029-30.

Earlier this year, the broadcaster extended its rights to Italian soccer’s top-tier Serie A and also provides coverage of the pan-European UEFA Women's Champions League. TV4 will also show next year’s flagship FIFA Women’s World Cup.

Across other sports, meanwhile, it holds rights to the current cycle of the Olympic Games, as well as tennis and motorsports.

title: Host City 2026 to bring global event leaders to Glasgow to shape the future of major events
LPGA to replace Japan Classic with Konami-backed event
article_text:
Women’s golf’s top-tier LPGA has announced that its tournament in Japan will be revamped next year with a larger prize purse and title sponsorship from Japanese video game developer Konami.

The Konami Championship replaces the LPGA’s Toto Japan Classic in 2027 and will be held over four days, from November 4 to 7, at Taiheiyo Club’s Minori Course in Omitama, Ibaraki Prefecture, Japan.

Combine business intelligence and editorial excellence to reach engaged professionals across 36 leading media platforms.

The tournament will feature 78 players – 43 from the LPGA Tour and 35 from the Japan Ladies Professional Golf Association (JLPGA) Tour.

Significantly, the new tournament will have an increased purse of $3 million, up from the $2.1 million offered at the Japan Classic, making it one of the highest-paying women’s golf tournaments held in Japan.

Alongside prize money of $450,000, the winner will receive a two-year LPGA Tour card for the following year.

Kimihiko Higashio, chief executive of Konami Group Corporation, said: “This tournament has grown steadily since 1973 as the only official LPGA Tour event held in Japan.

“We are honored to participate as the host and title sponsor of a tournament with a long history and tradition. Konami Group is exploring new ways to realize our corporate purpose of ‘Experience Well-being Moments’ through games, sports, and various entertainment fields.”

The announcement comes as the LPGA continues to consolidate its 2027 calendar, having unveiled a revamp for its Championship tournament in the UK, with the LPGA co-sanctioning the event with the Ladies European Tour (LET), and Golf Saudi providing financial backing.

The Championship, played between July 19 and 25, appears to be taking the place of the Women’s Scottish Open, which is reportedly no longer on the LPGA schedule, and will have an overall prize purse of $4 million.

The tour’s ongoing 2026 season features 33 events across 13 countries and a record total prize purse of over $132 million.

For Konami, the new title sponsorship adds to its visibility within sport, having signed up this year as a global sponsor to this year’s 2026 World Baseball Classic (WBC) national teams competition.

The Japanese developer has an extensive soccer portfolio, which includes a licensing deal with the French Football Federation national body, major European clubs such as AC Milan, Arsenal, Barcelona, Borussia Dortmund, Inter Milan, and Manchester United, as well as the top-flight J.League domestically.

title: Perfect Game expands youth baseball platform into GCC
article_text:
Perfect Game, the world’s largest youth baseball and softball platform and scouting service, has announced its expansion into the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) region, naming VICE Baseball as its Country Partner for the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Kuwait.

The announcement comes one week after Perfect Game revealed its new partnership in China, continuing the organisation’s international growth.

Beginning in December 2026, VICE will roll out Perfect Game tournaments, clinics and showcases across all four countries.

Dubai will host the first event, followed by a major international tournament in March 2027 that will bring together teams from around the world.

The goal is to strengthen the region’s baseball community and give young athletes more opportunities to compete and showcase their skills in front of scouts.

VICE Baseball, a subsidiary of VICE Sports Group led by Tony Khoury, is a US-based youth baseball development organisation with roots in Katy, Texas.

As Perfect Game’s partner across the GCC, VICE will pair its player development experience with Perfect Game’s established tournament and scouting platform.

VICE’s baseball operations are led by David McDaniel, who brings more than 20 years of coaching experience.

McDaniel played professionally as a catcher in the Cleveland Indians, Detroit Tigers and Texas Rangers organisations.

He later coached with the Sugar Land Skeeters (now the Sugar Land Space Cowboys) and helped guide Texas high school teams to state championships.

His approach emphasises sound fundamentals, game awareness and leadership to prepare players for higher levels of competition.

Kash Shaikh, Perfect Game’s Chief Marketing Officer and Head of International, is the former chairman, CEO and co-founder of Dubai-based Baseball United.

"It’s very special to be able to bring more baseball back to Dubai, Saudi, and the surrounding GCC region. After spending the last four years in Dubai working to build the baseball ecosystem with my previous league, I realised that we needed to do more to help a greater number of young athletes fall in love with the game," said Shaikh.

"With PG and our partnership with VICE, we will now offer families across the region access to top tournaments, international events and the best baseball scouting platform in the world. There are a lot of people already doing great work in the baseball community, and we are looking forward to partnering with them to make it all happen," he added.

VICE will work with local baseball organisations, academies and teams to build a regular event calendar and encourage participation across age groups.

Showcases will give players a chance to demonstrate their skills and gain visibility through Perfect Game’s international platform.

The long-term goal is a sustainable regional circuit that brings baseball communities together, raises the level of competition and gives young athletes a clearer path to advance in the sport.

"Our partnership with Perfect Game marks a milestone for youth baseball in the GCC. It puts a spotlight on the talent here and gives young players a new platform to compete at a higher level and showcase their skills," said Khoury.

"College coaches and professional scouts will have direct access to player profiles and stats through Perfect Game, and we expect some to attend future events in the region. That gives our players the same kind of scouting exposure as players in the US. We’re grateful for Perfect Game’s trust in VICE and the chance to build something lasting for players and families across the region."

Event dates, locations and registration details will be announced at PerfectGame.org.

title: Maincast Sport secures WTA broadcast rights in Ukraine
article_text:
Maincast Sport has acquired the rights to broadcast the WTA Tour Driven by Mercedes-Benz in Ukraine under a long-term agreement, bringing the world's leading women's professional tennis tour to Ukrainian audiences with dedicated Ukrainian-language coverage.

The agreement will give fans access to Ukrainian-language coverage of WTA tournaments throughout the 2027 season, as the Tour visits 26 countries and territories. From Brisbane and Auckland in January, the season will take in iconic destinations including Indian Wells, Miami, Madrid, Rome and Beijing, culminating in the season-ending FAGE WTA Finals in Charlotte, USA, in November.

The WTA Tour joins Maincast Sport’s portfolio of international sports properties including the NBA, Copa del Rey, MotoGP and NASCAR. Now with the WTA, the addition further strengthens Maincast Sport’s offering, bringing fans world-class women’s tennis and the opportunity to follow the Ukrainian players who consistently compete at the highest level.

The partnership includes: International WTA 1000 events, WTA 500 Events, WTA 250 Events, and the FAGE WTA Finals taking place in Charlotte (USA), where the season’s top eight singles players and doubles teams will compete.

“Tennis is one of the sports where Ukraine has genuine stars, and fans have followed every match our players have played for years. From 2027, matches featuring Elina Svitolina, Marta Kostyuk, Dayana Yastremska and other Ukrainian players will be available exclusively on Maincast Sport, alongside hundreds of matches from the world’s best players. We’re creating our own tennis shows, analysis and broadcasts with star guests. The WTA calendar runs almost all year round, so Maincast Sport viewers will get top-level tennis every week,,” said Vitalii Volochai, co-founder of Maincast.

“We’re delighted to partner with Maincast Sport to bring more women’s tennis to fans in Ukraine, where the sport already means so much. Ukrainian players continue to make an important impact on the global stage, and this agreement will give fans more opportunities to follow their favourite athletes and experience the excitement of the WTA Tour throughout the season,” said Marina Storti, CEO of WTA Ventures.

WTA Tour matches will be available to fans on the Maincast Sport TV channel and Maincast.tv platform.

title: Friday Night 5G Lights: 5 Takeaways From Our Sit-Down With T-Mobile’s Kaley Gagnon
article_text:
The business of youth sports, first in your search results.

T-Mobile’s Friday Night 5G Lights awarded more than $8.4 million to high schools in 2026, its third season, and more than $16 million since its 2024 launch, according to T-Mobile. YSBR sat down with Kaley Gagnon, Vice President of Marketing at T-Mobile, for an episode of the Jr. Sports Marketing podcast to talk about where the program came from and what it has done for the business.

We recorded before the 2026 field was cut to 40 Division Finalists. Since then, Menasha High School in Menasha, Wis., has won the $1 million grand prize, T-Mobile announced November 12.

Gagnon has spent nearly 20 years in telecom, she said, and joined T-Mobile about five years ago to launch and scale its 5G Home Internet product. She grew up an Air Force kid who moved often. The constant, in her words, was Friday night football, and the Airheads from the concession stand.

Here are five takeaways from our conversation.

1. T-Mobile’s Sports Strategy Starts With the Experience, Not the Logo

T-Mobile’s mission is to be the best in the world at connecting people to their world, Gagnon said, and few things are more central to people’s worlds than sports and entertainment. “It was less about, let’s put our logo and the color magenta on the back of the wall,” she said. “It was more about how do we make the experience better for consumers and for our members.”

She described three pillars. The first is the network inside the game. She cited Major League Baseball’s automated ball-strike system, where a tap of the helmet now signals a challenge, as an example of network integration changing how a sport is played.

The second is member perks. Club Magenta gives T-Mobile customers a place to rest, recharge and skip the line at events like Lollapalooza in Chicago. Gagnon called it “that little bit of pixie dust on top.”

The third is community, through programs like Friday Night 5G Lights and T-Mobile’s partnership with Little League, aimed at making youth sports more accessible.

2. Friday Night 5G Lights Started as a Small-Town Business Problem

Gagnon was direct about the origin. T-Mobile was growing nationally but finding growth harder in smaller towns, she said, even after millions of dollars in network investment and new stores in those markets.

The team called it a gap between perception and reality. “The perception was still maybe that T-Mobile wasn’t a brand in their community, wasn’t a brand that was going to work for them, even though the reality was there and the proof was there,” she said.

So the team went into those communities and talked with the mobile experts who staff T-Mobile stores there, looking for one thing every town shared that the company could invest in at scale. The answer came at the end of an afternoon conversation, when someone asked a rep about evening plans. The reply: the high school football game.

“That is where everybody comes together. It’s the social event of the week,” Gagnon said. “When we make a commitment, we don’t go small.”

3. How Does Friday Night 5G Lights Work?

Big sweepstakes can scare small communities off entirely, Gagnon said, because they assume they will never be the one. The first design principle was spreading the money. “We want a lot of communities and schools to benefit from this program,” she said.

The mechanic is apply, post, win. Every social post with the program’s hashtag, #FN5GL, counts as an entry into $5K Fridays, with winners drawn weekly. In 2026, 1,000 schools received $5,000 each, according to T-Mobile. “$5,000 goes such a long way in making a difference in these communities,” Gagnon said.

Public voting takes over from there. This season added four geographic divisions, which Gagnon compared to conference rivalries in college sports. T-Mobile narrowed more than 2,400 applications to 40 Division Finalists at $25,000 each, then to four Division Champions in the West, Midwest, South and East at $250,000 each, the company said. Those four competed for the $1 million field upgrade. Gagnon said there were 25 finalists in 2025.

Communities supply the rest. The 2025 champion, Dierks High School in Arkansas, won with nearly 2 million votes from a town of 884 people, according to T-Mobile. Gagnon said Dierks’ rival football team put the voting QR code on its jumbotron and took timeouts for voting, and 2024 winner Inola High School in Oklahoma sent supporters by bus to Tulsa to hand out QR codes.

4. Credibility First, Then Growth That Outlasts the Season

T-Mobile’s core product is reliability, Gagnon said, so credibility has to come before any pitch. “It’s very easy for big brands to come in with the blunt instrument and slap their logo everywhere and say, ‘We’re here, you’re welcome,'” she said. “That’s not our brand.”

She placed the program at the top of a traditional marketing funnel. “Before you start selling me on something, make me believe that it’s going to work for me and make me believe that you’re a brand that actually cares who I am in my community,” she said.

The program rarely talks about coverage, yet Gagnon said it has opened people’s minds to giving T-Mobile a look. In the communities T-Mobile tracked, deeper engagement, from $5K Fridays through the later rounds, lined up with more business growth, she said, “not just during the program, but over time after the program.” She did not share specific figures.

title: Baller League launches international women’s competition
article_text:
Baller League has introduced a women’s competition as part of its new Nations Cup, creating an international six-a-side tournament for amateur female players across 16 countries and 64 cities.

The women’s tournament will run alongside a men’s competition, with both winning teams receiving equal $1m prizes. Teams will progress from city-level tournaments to national qualifiers before the 16 national champions compete at the international finals.

The format will allow amateur teams to enter without affiliation to a professional club, academy or agent. Registration is scheduled to open in March 2027, with the competition running from 26th June until the final weekend from 5th-7th November.

The introduction of the women’s tournament represents an expansion of Baller League’s existing six-a-side format. Founded in Germany in 2024, the competition has since established leagues in the UK and United States.

The equal prize allocation means a combined $2m will be awarded to the men’s and women’s champions. Baller League founder and CEO Felix Starck has described each $1m award as what the organisation believes to be the largest prize offered to amateur footballers, although that claim has not been independently verified.

For the UK, the Nations Cup will build on Baller League’s existing domestic presence and provide amateur women’s teams with a route from local competition to representing their country in an international tournament.

title: Arab Cup Qatar 2025 wins Premier Sports Event of the Year Award
article_text:
The FIFA Arab Cup Qatar 2025 won the Qatar Tourism Award for Premier Sports Event of the Year, in recognition of the tournament's outstanding success, strong fan turnout, and contributions to Qatar's economy and tourism sector.

The Local Organizing Committee for Football Events received the award at a ceremony held in Doha, which recognized leading events that have helped strengthen Qatar's position as a premier destination for hosting major sporting events.

The tournament was held from Dec 1 to 18, 2025, with 16 Arab national teams competing across six stadiums that had previously hosted matches during the FIFA World Cup Qatar 2022. A total of 1,220,063 fans attended the 32 matches. The final, held at Lusail Stadium, drew 84,517 spectators, setting a record for the highest attendance in the tournament's history.

The tournament's success extended beyond the sporting arena and fan engagement to include a boost to tourism and economic activity. An economic impact assessment conducted in collaboration with Nielsen Sports, a company specializing in sports analytics, found that the tournament generated a total economic impact of QR2.89 billion for the local economy.

The tournament formed part of an exceptional football season in Qatar in 2025, during which the country hosted the finals of three FIFA competitions within three weeks. These included the inaugural 48-team edition of the FIFA U-17 World Cup Qatar and the FIFA Intercontinental Cup.

Qatar is currently hosting the FIFA U-17 World Cup Qatar 2026 and is preparing to host the final three matches of the FIFA Intercontinental Cup 2026, scheduled for Dec 9, 12 and 16.

Qatar continues to strengthen its presence on the global sporting stage by hosting a series of major international competitions, including the FIBA Basketball World Cup 2027, the FIFA Arab Cup 2029, the FIVB Volleyball World Championship 2029 and the Asian Games 2030.

title: Athlete Image Rights Saudi Arabia: A 2026 Playbook for Clubs, Sponsors and Players
article_text:
If you sign, sponsor or manage athletes in the Kingdom, athlete image rights saudi arabia is now a commercial issue you cannot leave to the small print. The new Sports Law and the creation of the Saudi Center for Sports Arbitration (SCSA) change how likeness, endorsement and merchandising deals are built and enforced. Every commercial use of a player's name, face, voice or biometric likeness should now trace back to a written licence. This guide takes a clear position on which licensing model to choose, which forum to use for disputes and which clauses to insist on, rather than listing every option and leaving the decision to you.

It is written for people who need to act. Practical views reflect market practice and the way the rules are interpreted, and statutory points are anchored to primary sources.

At a glance: how clubs, sponsors, agents and players can licence, protect and enforce image and likeness rights in Saudi Arabia after the 2026 Sports Law and SCSA reforms.

A player's persona is exploited commercially at the meeting point of contract law, intellectual property, privacy and the sport-specific framework introduced in 2026. Before any deal, you need to know where the right comes from and who is entitled to grant it.

The new Sports Law was issued by Royal Decree No. M/121 dated 10/06/1447H and came into force in June 2026. It modernises how sport is governed in Saudi Arabia and replaces the earlier framework. For commercial parties, the key point is that it formalises sports dispute resolution through the SCSA. It also clarifies commercial governance across clubs and federations and steers sports-related disputes, including many image-rights and commercial matters, towards a specialist forum.

In practice this has two consequences. Contracts should be drafted with SCSA arbitration in mind, and existing commercial rights structures should be reviewed against the updated governance expectations. Where a licence touches player registration, league participation or federation-level rights, contractual clarity matters even more.

Saudi law does not create a single, standalone "image right" of the kind found in some Western publicity-rights statutes. Protection is assembled from several overlapping sources:

- Intellectual property: trademarks over names and logos, and copyright in photographs and designs.

The Saudi Authority for Intellectual Property (SAIP) administers trademark and copyright registration and offers enforcement routes. These are highly relevant where a likeness is fixed in a logo, a product design or a copyrighted image. Because no automatic statutory monopoly covers a player's persona, the written licence carries the commercial weight, and its scope sets the limits of what each party may do.

Cross-border deals add a further layer. Where clubs or sponsors operate in several jurisdictions, FIFA governance principles and international IP norms, including WIPO guidance on personality and publicity rights, influence how player commercial rights are allocated and how clashes with federation or league rights are handled. Foreign sponsors should reconcile Saudi contract mechanics with these expectations from the start.

Who owns and who can license a player's image?

Owning a likeness and exploiting it are different things. A player generally holds the personal interest in their own image, but the right to exploit it commercially can be shared, assigned or restricted through employment contracts, league rules and agency arrangements. Getting the chain of authority right separates an enforceable licence from an expensive dispute.

Under Saudi player contracts and league frameworks, clubs often secure a defined share of a player's commercial rights. These typically cover collective, team-context uses such as squad photography, kit imagery and stadium activations, while the player keeps individual endorsement rights. The boundary is set by the contract and the applicable league rules, not by any default law.

A club that wants to build a solo campaign around a star player's face needs express contractual authority, because a general employment relationship does not supply it. Sponsors dealing with a club should check that it really holds the specific rights it offers, especially for individual rather than team use.

Agents commonly negotiate and, where authorised, assign or sub-license player image rights. Any third-party licence must lead back to a valid grant of authority, such as a power of attorney, an agency mandate or an express contractual permission. Where FIFA or league clearance affects a player's status, sponsors should confirm that the commercial arrangements do not collide with registration or transfer restrictions. Unclear agency authority is among the most frequent causes of later disputes.

Minors call for extra care. A guardian should give consent to use a minor's image, it should be documented in writing, and the scope and duration should be narrower. Data and privacy protections bite particularly hard for minors, so any licence should include enhanced approval rights and clear termination triggers. Sponsors are best advised to treat minor image licensing as its own higher-risk category, not as a variant of an adult deal.

This is the stage at which deals are won or lost. The model you pick determines control, revenue, administrative load and how easily you can enforce. Below are the main licence types, the clauses that matter, the payment structures, a side-by-side comparison and a decision framework.

- Exclusive licence. The sponsor or partner takes sole rights to use the athlete's likeness within a set product category, territory and term. Best for flagship brand campaigns and sole merchandising partnerships.

- Non-exclusive licence. The player can license the same likeness to several parties. Best for spreading revenue and testing emerging markets.
